interviewQuestions.question: Explain write-through vs write-back caching, and when you'd pick one over the other.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Write-through sends every write straight to the next level down as it happens, so the cache and memory are never out of sync — trivial to reason about and safe against data loss, but a write-heavy loop that updates the same address a thousand times generates a thousand writes to memory even though only the final value ever mattered. Write-back keeps writes local: it updates the line in cache and marks it dirty, deferring the write to memory until the line is evicted — those same thousand writes collapse into one eventual write-back, at the cost of needing a dirty bit per line and careful handling to make sure a dirty line's data isn't lost or read stale from memory by another agent.

Most CPU data caches default to write-back, because real programs write the same stack slots, loop counters, and object fields repeatedly before moving on — write-back captures that reuse and cuts memory traffic dramatically. Write-through fits where consistency with the next level matters more than write traffic: some designs use it for outer cache levels talking to memory-mapped I/O or in systems where multiple agents must observe writes immediately without waiting for an eviction.

The multicore wrinkle worth mentioning: write-back interacts directly with coherence protocols like MESI — a dirty line effectively means "the authoritative copy of this data isn't in memory right now," which is exactly why a coherence protocol has to be able to force a write-back (or forward the dirty data directly) when another core requests that address.

**Testing:** whether you connect the trade-off to *why* write-back dominates in real CPUs, and can name the coherence interaction.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Write-through vs write-back

interviewQuestions.question: What is write-allocate vs no-write-allocate, and why do write-back caches almost always pair with write-allocate?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This is the separate decision of what happens on a **write miss** — writing to an address that isn't currently in the cache. Write-allocate pulls the whole block into the cache first (like a read miss would), then applies the write to the now-resident line. No-write-allocate writes straight through to the next level and doesn't bring the block into the cache at all, leaving the cache untouched by that write.

The pairing that shows up almost everywhere is write-back + write-allocate: since write-back's entire point is capturing repeated writes to the same line cheaply, it needs the line resident to do that — a write-allocate miss brings it in once, and every subsequent write to that line (and any read, since it's now warm too) becomes a cheap hit. Pairing write-back with no-write-allocate would mostly defeat the purpose: you'd write straight through on the first touch and then still have to fetch the block separately if you wanted to read it, missing the whole reuse benefit.

The other common pairing is write-through + no-write-allocate: since write-through is going to write to memory regardless, there's little benefit to also caching a block you only wrote once and might never read — it would just occupy space and potentially evict a more useful line. This pairing shows up in caches optimized for write-heavy, read-rarely patterns, like some write-combining buffers used for streaming stores to non-cacheable-adjacent memory regions.

**Testing:** whether you can explain why these two policies pair the way they do, rather than treating write-allocate as an independent, arbitrary choice.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The write-miss decision

interviewQuestions.question: A dirty line in a write-back cache is silently corrupted by a hardware fault before it's evicted. What does this expose about write-back's risk profile compared to write-through, and how do real systems mitigate it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Write-back's core trade — deferring the actual write to memory — means the *only* authoritative copy of that data exists in the cache for however long the line stays dirty and resident. If that line is corrupted, misdirected, or simply lost (power loss to volatile SRAM, an uncorrected bit flip) before it's ever written back, the update is gone permanently with no trace in memory at all. Write-through never has this exposure window, because memory is updated synchronously with every write — the cache is a pure accelerator for reads, never the sole owner of unwritten state.

This is exactly why write-back caches at scale pair with ECC (error-correcting codes) on cache SRAM, not just on DRAM — a single-bit flip in a dirty line is correctable in flight rather than silently persisted as wrong data with no memory-side copy to catch it. It's also why systems with strict durability requirements (databases doing log writes, storage controllers) either bypass write-back caching for that specific path (write-through or explicitly flushed/non-temporal stores) or pair it with battery-backed or capacitor-backed cache (common in RAID/storage controllers) so a dirty line survives a power loss long enough to be flushed.

The broader senior-level point: write-back is a *performance* optimization that trades a small, real durability/fault window for large write-traffic savings, and the systems that can't accept that window (durability-critical writes, or hardware without ECC on the cache SRAM itself) either avoid write-back on that path or add explicit protection rather than accepting the risk silently.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about write-back's failure/durability exposure as a genuine design cost, not just its performance upside.
